questions.title: Why does QLoRA still need a 16‑bit computation data type when the base model is 4‑bit?
questions.question_body: In the QLoRA description the weights are stored in a 4‑bit NF4 data type and are dequantized to BF16 for computation. I’m confused why we don’t perform all forward and backward passes directly in BF16 and then re‑quantize the updated weights back to NF4. Is the extra storage of BF16 before back‑propagation necessary for gradient accuracy, or does it introduce any loss? How does this choice affect the memory budget compared to a pure 4‑bit implementation?

questions.title: How does Double Quantization reduce the memory overhead of quantization constants?
questions.question_body: The paper describes quantizing the first‑level constants $c_2^{	ext{FP32}}$ to 8‑bit floats and then applying a second level of constants $c_1^{	ext{FP32}}$. Can someone explain how this two‑stage process halves the average bits per parameter? A simple calculation with block sizes 64 for $W$ and 256 for $c_2$ would be helpful.

questions.title: What is the intuition behind using a NormalFloat (NF) data type instead of standard Float4?
questions.question_body: NF4 is introduced as an information‑theoretically optimal quantization for normally distributed weights. Why does matching quantile distribution to a normal already give better empirical results than plain 4‑bit floating point? Is there an intuitive explanation for why NF4 achieves higher accuracy?

questions.title: Why are LoRA adapters needed on *every* transformer layer to recover full‑finetuning performance?
questions.question_body: Figure 3 shows that using adapters only on query/value projections leads to degraded performance, whereas adding adapters to all layers restores performance. Intuitively, I would expect that adapting only the most important matrices (e.g., attention) should be enough. What is happening with the remaining layers that requires adapter updates everywhere when using the frozen quantized base?

questions.title: How does QLoRA handle back‑propagation through frozen quantized weights?
questions.question_body: The update rule for LoRA involves computing $ rac{ ackslashpartial 	extbf{X}}{ ackslashpartial 	extbf{W}}$ during adapter training. Since $	extbf{W}$ is stored in NF4, we must first dequantize it to BF16 before gradient computation. Does this dequantization introduce any approximation error during backpropagation? Does QLoRA store any intermediate activations related to $	extbf{W}$ that might affect memory usage or compute time?

questions.title: What causes Paged Optimizers to eliminate memory spikes during gradient checkpointing?
questions.question_body: "Paged Optimizers" refer to using NVIDIA unified memory to move optimizer state between GPU RAM and host RAM. However, gradient checkpointing can still cause out‑of‑memory errors if a large activation needs to be restored. How exactly does paging mitigate this without impacting training speed, and in which regimes (sequence length, batch size) do we see noticeable slowdown?

questions.title: `k‐bit` QLoRA vs `k‐bit` Full Finetuning: Why do we recover full precision after adapter tuning?
questions.question_body: Table 5 shows that performing only adapter tuning on a fully quantized (NF4) base restores performance equal to full 16‑bit fine‐tuning. Intuitively I thought significant information loss could not be recovered by training only a few new parameters. How can low‐rank adapters compensate for such heavy quantization errors across all layers?

questions.title: `NFk` construction uses two ranges with one zero removed – what are the practical consequences?
questions.question_body: The NFk datatype is built by interpolating $2^{k-1}$ negative and $2^{k-1}+1$ positive Chebyshev points and then removing one zero. Why remove one zero instead of keeping both? What impact does this have on symmetry of quantization bins, handling of padding tokens, or representational bias?

questions.title: `k`=4 NF4 vs FP4: Are there scenarios where FP4 outperforms NF4?
questions.question_body: "Double Quantization did not degrade performance" but how do we know that there isn’t any hidden loss? Could there be tasks or architectures (e.g., encoder‑decoder) where FP4 actually provides better calibration because of its asymmetric range? Has anyone benchmarked per‑metric differences beyond perplexity/GLUE/mmlu?
